newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Russia oil product export to East Asia set to fall.
newsitem.headline: Russia oil product export to East Asia set to fall.

text.p: Russian oil product exports to East Asia are expected to fall further over the next two years because of meagre refinery runs and creaking export infrastructure, industry sources said on Thursday.
"The importance of Russian exports to Asia is decreasing," a regional trader said.
"There is the problem of refineries only working at 50 percent capacity. Russian exports are unprofitable for refineries... A lot of time the exports are done purely for generating hard currency."

He said there were about 20 refineries in Russia, but only one or two ran at more than 50 percent capacity while some were operating as low as 30 to 40 percent, due to limited cash flow to pay for crude.
Sources said Russia's eastern ports had the capacity to handle between six million and eight million tonnes per year for exports to East Asia.
But they managed only three million to four million tonnes of exports in 1996, down about 30 percent from the previous year, they said.

Sales to East Asia this year are expected to hover around three million tonnes, comprising 0.5 or 0.25 percent sulphur diesel, M-100/M-40 fuel oil, which is almost equivalent to the 180-centistoke grade, and A-76 or 83-octane leaded gasoline.

China takes about 60 percent of Russia's exports to East Asia, mostly diesel and fuel oil. Japan imports 10-15 percent, Vietnam 10 percent, while the remaining 10-15 percent is exported to the Korean peninsula.

Russian gasoline almost dominated Vietnam's market but the low quality made it unattractive to most other Asian buyers, which were being fed higher specification material from Thailand, South Korea and Singapore, sources said.

Eugene Khartukov, of Moscow's independent International Centre for Petroleum Business Studies, said during a recent conference in Singapore that most Russian refineries were basic, which limited their capacity to produce premium products.

The refineries' yield was therefore dominated by heavy fuel oil (35-40 percent) while the more valuable lighter products such as diesel, gasoline, kerosene and naphtha accounted for about half of refinery output, he said.

A trading source said that despite the higher fuel oil output, exports of the product were limited by high rail freight costs, whereas diesel and gasoline achieved higher export prices which offset the rail costs.
Khartukov said the Russian government announced a nationwide refinery modernisation plan in 1992 to lift oil processing capacity to 82-85 percent of capacity.
But it would take 12-14 years to implement the programme and the country's refineries would at best achieve 64 percent capacity by the end of 1997, he said.
Industry sources said Russia's East Asian exports were also choked by the rickety rail system and port facilities.

"For the past five years there has been no direct investment into the (port) terminals and rail systems," a trader familiar with Russia said. "Moscow has a hands-off approach and these facilities have to stand on their own."
